purpose: Venetoclax is used to treat certain types of blood cancers, including chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). It is often used alone or combined with other cancer medicines. Your doctor chose this medication because it specifically targets the type of cancer cells in your body.
how_it_works: Cancer cells often survive longer than they should because they have a protein called BCL-2 that blocks their natural death process. Venetoclax works by blocking that BCL-2 protein, which signals the cancer cells to die on their own. Think of it like removing a shield that was protecting the cancer cells from being destroyed.
common_side_effects: Nausea, diarrhea, and vomiting are very common, especially early on. You may also feel very tired, have low blood counts (which can make you more prone to infections or bruising), constipation, or swelling in your hands and feet. Tell your doctor or pharmacist if any of these bother you.
warnings: The most important warning is a serious condition called Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS), which can happen when many cancer cells die quickly and release harmful substances into your blood. This is why your dose is started very low and slowly increased. You will need blood tests and may need extra fluids before and during treatment. Also, this medicine lowers your immune system, so avoid people who are sick and report any fever right away. Do not take it with certain medications like antifungals or some antibiotics without checking first, and avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice.
typical_dosing: Venetoclax is taken by mouth once a day with a meal and water. Your doctor will start you on a low dose, usually 20 mg per day, and slowly increase it over 5 weeks up to the full dose of 400 mg per day. This slow increase helps protect you from Tumor Lysis Syndrome. Always take it at the same time each day and never skip or double up on doses.
